common_name: Fatalii Red Pepper (Red Central African Superhot)

planting.note: Start seed indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before the last frost; Capsicum chinense superhots are slow and erratic to germinate without steady warmth.

directions: Fatalii Red is the red-ripening sibling of the classic Central African yellow Fatalii, sharing its sharp, citrusy flavor but ripening to a glossy red instead of pale yellow. Expect roughly 125,000-325,000 Scoville heat units, noticeably hotter and more acidic-tasting than a standard habanero, so handle ripe pods with gloves. Start seed indoors on a heat mat, since this variety germinates slowly even by chinense standards, and give it a long, warm season outdoors in full sun. The thin-walled, elongated pods dry and powder well, making this a favorite for hot sauce makers who want bright citrus heat rather than the sweeter, fruitier notes of a habanero.
sources: Trade Winds Fruit - Fatalii Red Pepper Seeds
Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

planting.note: Start seed indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before the last frost, then harden off only after nights stay reliably warm.

directions: Chocolate Fatalii ripens to a glossy chocolate-brown pod and carries roughly 125,000-325,000+ Scoville heat units, in the same intense range as a habanero but with a smokier, earthier, more floral background flavor than the sharply citrusy yellow Fatalii. Start seed indoors on a heat mat well ahead of the last frost, since germination is slow and uneven in cool soil, then transplant into full sun only after nights stay warm. Pods ripen from green through brown over a long season, so give it the longest warm window your climate allows. Dark pods can be harder to judge for ripeness than red or yellow superhots, so squeeze gently for firmness rather than relying on color alone before harvesting for sauces or drying.
sources: Pepper Joe's - Chocolate Fatalii Pepper Seeds
Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

common_name: Red Scotch Bonnet Pepper (Caribbean Red-Ripening Scotch Bonnet)

planting.note: Start indoors on a heat mat; transplant into warm soil once nights stay reliably above 60°F.

directions: This Scotch Bonnet selection ripens from green to a deep red instead of the more familiar yellow or orange, with the same squat, crinkled bonnet-shaped pods and a heat level in the typical Scotch Bonnet range of roughly 100,000-350,000 Scoville units, comparable to a habanero. Its fruity, slightly sweet flavor makes it a staple of Jamaican and wider Caribbean jerk seasoning, pepper sauces, and stews. Start seed indoors with bottom heat, since chinense types germinate slowly, and transplant into full sun once the weather is reliably warm. Plants are compact and heavily productive, so stake or cage them once fruit load builds to keep brittle branches from snapping.
sources: True Leaf Market / Mountain Valley Seed Company - Red Scotch Bonnet Seeds
Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

common_name: Chocolate Scotch Bonnet Pepper (Caribbean Brown-Ripening Scotch Bonnet)

planting.note: Start indoors on a heat mat; transplant into warm soil once nights stay reliably above 60°F.

directions: The chocolate-brown form of Scotch Bonnet carries the classic lantern-shaped, crinkled pod and is generally considered a bit hotter and more earthy-tasting than the standard yellow type, landing in a similar 100,000-350,000 Scoville range but with a deeper, smokier edge. It is widely used in Caribbean jerk marinades, hot sauces, and seasoning blends where its darker color and richer flavor are prized. Sow indoors on a heat mat well before the last frost, as germination is slow, and move plants to full sun only once nights stay warm. Compact, bushy plants bear heavily over a long season, so plan on steady harvest through summer and fall.
sources: Reimer Seeds - Chocolate Scotch Bonnet Pepper Seeds
Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

common_name: Hainan Yellow Lantern Chili (Chinese Yellow Emperor Chili)

planting.note: Start indoors on a heat mat; this chinense type needs warm soil and a long season to size up its lantern-shaped pods.

directions: Native to Hainan Island in southern China, this habanero-type chinense ripens to a bright yellow, lantern-shaped pod carrying roughly 300,000 Scoville heat units, squarely in habanero-to-superhot territory, well beyond the typical jalapeno or Thai chile grown in most home gardens. Its sharp, fruity heat is traditionally fermented with salt and garlic into the distinctive yellow lantern chili sauce popular along the Hainan coast. Start seed indoors on a heat mat, since chinense types are slow to germinate, and give plants a long, warm growing season in full sun to fully ripen the thick-walled pods. Harvest continually through summer and fall for fresh use or fermenting, wearing gloves to handle the ripe fruit.
sources: Wikipedia - Hainan yellow lantern chili (horticultural and culinary background)
Patrick's Pepper Patch - Hainan Yellow Lantern seeds
Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

planting.note: Start on a heat mat 10-12 weeks before the last frost; superhot chinense types need a long head start and steady warmth to germinate.

directions: 7 Pot Yellow is a Trinidadian superhot that ripens from green to a bright yellow, wrinkled, habanero-shaped pod and is rated near 950,000 Scoville heat units, placing it alongside the Bhut Jolokia and Trinidad Scorpion among the world's hottest peppers and well above its red 7 Pot and Trinidad Scorpion cousins already common in backyard pepper collections. The name reflects the Trinidadian claim that a single pod can season seven pots of stew. Start seed indoors on a heat mat, since germination is slow even by superhot standards, and transplant into full sun only once nights are reliably warm. Fruity, floral flavor underlies the intense heat, making it popular for small-batch hot sauces and powders; always handle ripe pods with gloves.
sources: Trade Winds Fruit - 7 Pot Pepper, Yellow Seeds
Reimer Seeds - 7 Pot Yellow Pepper Seeds
